title: Centre of Gravity
page_title: Centre of gravity - IGCSE Physics Revision Notes

blocks.name: Centre of gravity
blocks.definition: State what is meant by centre of gravity

blocks.md: - The **centre of gravity** of an object is defined as:
**The point through which the weight of an object acts**

- For a symmetrical object of uniform density, the **centre of gravity is located at the point of symmetry**

  - For example, the centre of gravity of a sphere is at the centre

blocks.alt: Diagram of triangle, ellipse, trapezium and parallelogram with dashed symmetry lines meeting at each shape’s centre of gravity, shown by a downward purple arrow
blocks.caption: The centre of gravity of a regularly shaped object can be found using symmetry

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
Since the centre of gravity is a hypothetical point, it can lie inside or outside a body. The centre of gravity will constantly shift depending on the shape of a body. For example, a human body’s centre of gravity is lower when leaning forward than when standing upright

However, when you are drawing force diagrams, always draw the weight force as if it were acting from the centre of gravity of the object.

blocks.name: Stability
blocks.definition: Describe, qualitatively, the effect of the position of the centre of gravity on the stability of simple objects

blocks.md:
- The **position **of the centre of gravity affects the **stability **of an object
- An object is **stable **when its centre of gravity lies above its **base**
- If the centre of gravity does not lie above its base, it produces a moment that causes the object to **topple **over

blocks.alt: Two blue blocks on flat and sloping surfaces, each with a red downward arrow from a marked point showing the weight acting through the centre of mass
blocks.caption: The object will topple when its centre of gravity is no longer over its base

blocks.md:
- The most stable objects have a **low **centre of gravity and a **wide **base

  - Cars are stable because they have a low centre of gravity and a wide base

- Taller objects with a narrow base have a higher centre of gravity and are less stable

  - This is why high-sided vehicles such as lorries are sometimes advised to avoid exposed bridges on very windy days

blocks.alt: Diagram comparing two blocks. The left block has a narrow base and a high centre of gravity so it tips easily, but the right block has a wide base and a low centre of gravity so it remains more stable.
blocks.caption: When the object is positioned on its narrow base, it is less stable because its centre of gravity is higher

blocks.md: - If the line of action of the **weight **force lies outside the base of the object, there will be a **resultant moment,** and the body will topple

blocks.text: Car and bus on varying inclines

blocks.alt: A car on various inclined planes up to 60 degrees without toppling because the line of action of its weight still lies within its base. A bus is tilted to 45 degrees before the line of action of its weight lies outside its base.
blocks.caption: The car can be tilted to 60° without toppling, but the bus will topple at 45°

blocks.md:
- Tall objects with a narrow base will topple easily

  - Ten-pin bowling pins are designed specifically to topple easily
- The stability of objects can be increased by widening the base

  - High chairs are designed with a wide base so that they do not topple
  - Bunsen burners have a wide base to ensure they do not topple

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md: You must explicitly link the design choices of objects to the physics principles involved when explaining the stability of objects. For example, increasing the base area will lower the centre of gravity or increase the tipping angle required to knock the object over.
